title: A finite group scheme has a faithful regular matrix representation
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $G$ be a finite $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], and put $A=\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)$ and $d=\dim_kA$ [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. The action of $G$ on $A$ by right translation gives a homomorphism of group schemes $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(A)$ which is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Here $\operatorname{GL}(A)$ is the basis-independent form of [def-sc-general-linear-group], and $\operatorname{GL}(A)(R)=\operatorname{Aut}_R(A\otimes_kR)$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$; the tensor product uses [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. After choosing a $k$-basis of $A$, this says that the induced coordinate homomorphism
$$k[T_{ij}\ (1\leq i,j\leq d),\det(T)^{-1}]\longrightarrow A,\qquad T_{ij}\longmapsto u_{ij},$$
is surjective. It preserves evaluation at the identity: $\epsilon(u_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$, where $\epsilon:A\to k$ is evaluation at the identity and $\delta_{ij}$ is $1$ for $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. For every $k$-algebra $R$, the matrix $U=(u_{ij})$ specializes along $x:A\to R$ to $\rho_R(x)$, and $\rho_R(xy)=\rho_R(x)\rho_R(y)$. No commutativity or reducedness of $G$ is required.

source.place: Theorem 4.9 and proof, printed p.87; applied with the entire finite-dimensional coordinate algebra as regular subrepresentation, as in the proof of Proposition 11.32, printed p.221.

proof.text: By [def-sc-group-scheme], $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A$ finite-dimensional over $k$. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] to get the coordinate maps $\Delta,\epsilon,S$ and their coassociativity, two counit identities and two antipode identities. The map $\epsilon$ is unital, so $1_A\ne0$ and $d\geq1$. Choose a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ as in [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. Define $u_{ij}\in A$ by $\Delta(e_j)=\sum_i e_i\otimes u_{ij}$. These expansions are unique: if $e_i^*:A\to k$ are the coordinate functionals, the maps $e_i^*\otimes1$ recover each coefficient. More generally $A\otimes_kR\simeq R^d$ for every $k$-algebra $R$, by $\sum_i e_i\otimes r_i\leftrightarrow(r_i)$; the inverse identities follow by expanding $a=\sum_i e_i^*(a)e_i$ on pure tensors and using their spanning property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

source.place: Theorem 4.9, printed p.87, taking V=A; Remark 4.1, printed p.84, choice of basis and coefficient convention.

proof.text:
Expand coassociativity on $e_j$:
$$\sum_{i,r} e_r\otimes u_{ri}\otimes u_{ij}=\sum_i e_i\otimes\Delta(u_{ij}).$$
Applying $e_r^*$ to the first factor gives $\Delta(u_{rj})=\sum_i u_{ri}\otimes u_{ij}$. Applying $1\otimes\epsilon$ to $\Delta(e_j)$ instead gives $\sum_i e_i\epsilon(u_{ij})=e_j$, hence $\epsilon(u_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$. Both identities are direct consequences of the coassociativity and counit identities of [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]; coefficient extraction is the explicit inverse from Step 1.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, equations (24) and (25), specialized to the regular coaction Delta.

proof.text:
For a $k$-algebra $R$ and a point $x:A\to R$, define the $R$-linear map $t_x$ on pure tensors by
$$t_x(a\otimes r)=\sum a_{(1)}\otimes x(a_{(2)})r,\qquad \Delta(a)=\sum a_{(1)}\otimes a_{(2)}.$$
The tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] makes this well-defined, independently of the tensor presentation; its matrix in the basis from Step 1 is $U(x)=(x(u_{ij}))$. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf], the point $xy$ is $\mu_R(x\otimes y)\Delta$, the identity is the counit and the inverse of $x$ is $xS$. Thus Step 2 gives, entry by entry,
$$U(xy)_{ij}=\sum_r x(u_{ir})y(u_{rj})=(U(x)U(y))_{ij},\qquad U(1)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}.$$
Putting $y=xS$ or $x=yS$ proves that $U(xS)$ is a two-sided inverse of $U(x)$. Consequently $t_x\in\operatorname{Aut}_R(A\otimes_kR)$ and $t_{xy}=t_x t_y$. These formulas commute with every homomorphism $R\to R'$ since they use only finite sums and products.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, verification following (25); regular right-translation convention preceding Theorem 4.9, printed p.87.

proof.text:
Take $R=A$ and $x=1_A$ in Step 3, so $U=(u_{ij})$ has inverse $(S(u_{ij}))$. The square case of [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet] gives $\det(U)\det(S(U))=\det(I)=1$; here $\det(I)=1$ follows at once from the permutation formula [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], as every nonidentity permutation has a zero factor. Evaluation of the polynomial generators [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], followed by [lem-weil-pbc-ring-localization-universal-property], therefore defines
$$\phi:k[T_{ij},\det(T)^{-1}]\longrightarrow A,\quad T_{ij}\longmapsto u_{ij},\quad \det(T)^{-1}\longmapsto\det(U)^{-1}.$$
By [def-sc-general-linear-group] and [def-weil-affine-spectrum], $\operatorname{Spec}\phi$ is a morphism $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}_{d,k}$ whose points are exactly $U(x)$. Step 2 and the coordinate multiplication and identity maps of [def-sc-general-linear-group] show that $\phi$ respects them: equality on every $T_{ij}$ extends to the localization by uniqueness. The affine product identifications of [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] identify these coordinate equalities with the scheme multiplication and identity diagrams. Thus $\rho$ is a group-scheme homomorphism, not just a homomorphism on $k$-points. The chosen basis identifies $\operatorname{GL}_{d,k}(R)$ with $\operatorname{Aut}_R(A\otimes_kR)$ by conjugating matrices with the isomorphism of Step 1; hence it gives the required morphism to $\operatorname{GL}(A)$.

source.place: Remark 4.1 and Example 4.2, printed p.84; Theorem 4.9, printed p.87, coordinate map O(GL_V) -> A. Determinant-localization detail expanded.

proof.text:
Apply the other counit identity $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta=1_A$ from [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] to each $e_j$. It gives
$$e_j=\sum_i\epsilon(e_i)u_{ij}.$$
Every term on the right is in the image of $\phi$, since $\phi$ is a $k$-algebra map and $u_{ij}=\phi(T_{ij})$. Hence every basis vector is in its image. Explicitly, if $a=\sum_j c_j e_j$, then the polynomial $\sum_{i,j}c_j\epsilon(e_i)T_{ij}$ maps to $a$. This proves surjectivity without assuming that $G$ is commutative or reduced.

source.place: Theorem 4.9 and proof, printed p.87, displayed counit identity and surjectivity argument, with V=A.

proof.text: Both $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $\operatorname{GL}_{d,k}=\operatorname{Spec}k[T_{ij},\det(T)^{-1}]$ are affine. Apply clause (2) of [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-affine-cover-criterion] to the covering consisting of the entire target: its inverse image is $G$ and its section map is the surjective $\phi$ of Step 5. Thus $\rho$ is a closed immersion. To identify the action, let $R\to R'$ be any algebra map and let $z:A\to R'$ be an $R'$-point of $G$. Evaluating the pure-tensor formula of Step 3 gives $(t_xa)(z)=\sum z(a_{(1)})x(a_{(2)})=a(zx)$, where $x$ is first extended to $R'$. This is right translation, including on arbitrary algebra-valued points. Step 2 proves the stated identity evaluation, and Step 3 proves the specialization and product clauses for every $R$. Changing the chosen basis conjugates these same operators, so the morphism into $\operatorname{GL}(A)$ is the intrinsic right-translation action asserted in the item.
